passage: I sit in the third row and saw Irfan debate whether uniforms should be compulsory. He opened with a survey the class had run, twenty-two out of thirty who said comfort mattered more. Then Zoya from the other team made the point that uniforms reduce pressure to compete with clothes, and Irfan paused. He said, "That's fair, I hadn't looked at it that way. But I'd still argue that a few casual days would keep the benefit." He didn't shout. His voice stayed level while his foot tapped. The other side actually nodded at him. Whether he changed his own mind, I can't say. But he sounded like he was listening, and he still held his ground. Abhinav.

qa.q: What did Irfan open his debate with?
qa.a: He opened with a survey the class had run.

qa.q: What might Irfan's tapping foot and level voice suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he felt some nervous energy but was managing it, since his voice stayed level. Abhinav can't tell whether Irfan changed his mind.

qa.q: What did Irfan do that strengthened his argument?
qa.a: He acknowledged Zoya's good point and then defended his own view with a specific proposal.

qa.q: How might the other team have felt about being acknowledged?
qa.a: They probably felt heard and respected, which is why they nodded at him.

grounding: A teen builds an argument with evidence, acknowledges a good point and defends a view, seen by an observer.

passage:
Monday. In the family debate about homework hours, Bhupen talked over everyone and called his sister Alka's point "stupid". She stopped speaking. He won the shouting and lost the room.
Wednesday. Bhupen asked his teacher for two studies on sleep and school. He wrote three points down and one thing Alka might say back.
Saturday. At dinner he said, "Alka, you were right that some homework builds habits. I'd like to argue that shorter tasks work as well, and here's a study." Alka leaned forward. "Okay, show me." They spent an hour going through it. Nobody won, but Papa said it was the best conversation they'd had in months.

qa.q: What did Bhupen call Alka's point on Monday?
qa.a: He called it "stupid".

qa.q: Why did Bhupen prepare a point Alka might say back?
qa.a: He probably regretted calling her point stupid and losing the room on Monday, so he wanted to understand her view. It suggests he now cares about being fair as well as being right.

qa.q: What made the Saturday debate go better than Monday's?
qa.a: He used evidence, admitted a good point from Alka and stayed respectful instead of shouting.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt on Monday?
qa.a: She probably felt dismissed and silenced, which is why she stopped speaking.

grounding: A teen learns that debate skill includes evidence and acknowledging good points, and that ridicule and volume fail.

passage:
Nilesh, you want to win tomorrow's debate by making the other side look silly? Sit down. Your Noor Nani lost a debate that way.
At sixteen I was the loudest girl in our school in Lucknow. The topic was whether girls should play cricket at school. I was for it. My opponent, a quiet boy, gave one good point: our school had no proper ground, only a small courtyard.
Instead of answering it, I laughed and said, "Maybe he's worried he'll lose to us!" The hall laughed. I felt wonderful.
Then the judge asked me, "And the courtyard?" I had nothing. I lost.
Afterwards my teacher said, "You had evidence, Noor. You had the girls' matches in Delhi. You just needed to say, 'Fair point about the ground, here's how others managed.'"
I've never forgotten that. The laugh lasted a minute. The loss lasted a year.

qa.q: What was the opponent's good point?
qa.a: Our school had no proper ground, only a small courtyard.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when the hall laughed?
qa.a: Noor felt wonderful and triumphant for a moment, sure that ridicule had won the argument.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the debate, and what could Noor have done instead?
qa.a: The judge asking "And the courtyard?" showed Noor had no answer; acknowledging the fair point and using the evidence about other girls' matches would have been stronger.

qa.q: How might the quiet boy have felt when the hall laughed at him?
qa.a: The quiet boy probably felt embarrassed and belittled, even though his point was reasonable.

grounding: The elder's story shows that winning by ridicule is a pitfall and that acknowledging a good point with evidence makes a stronger debate.

passage:
The inter-class debate on "Should school uniforms be scrapped?" was supposed to have microphones. Five minutes before it began, the sound system died. Now every speaker had two minutes and a noisy hall.
Samir was arguing for keeping uniforms. Dilnaz spoke first against: uniforms cost families money every year and some kids feel they can't be themselves.
Samir's friends were already whispering, "Just shout her down, the hall can't hear anyway."
He stood, took a breath, and didn't shout. "Dilnaz is right about cost. That's a real problem. So my claim is: keep uniforms, but let the school run a second-hand uniform exchange. Our survey of forty students showed thirty felt less judged about clothes with uniforms."
The front rows leaned in to hear. A few people nodded.
Dilnaz caught his eye afterwards. "You took my point seriously. That was annoying," she said, grinning.

qa.q: How many minutes did every speaker get?
qa.a: Every speaker had two minutes.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz have been feeling when she called it annoying, grinning?
qa.a: Dilnaz seemed amused and a little impressed, feeling respected because Samir took her point seriously.

qa.q: Which choice of Samir's worked, and why?
qa.a: Acknowledging the cost point and then offering evidence and a solution worked better than shouting, because the audience leaned in to listen.

qa.q: What would change if Samir had shouted her down?
qa.a: In the noisy hall it might have looked strong briefly, but it would have ignored a fair point and lost the listeners' respect.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager defending a position with a claim and evidence and acknowledging an opponent's good point rather than winning by volume.

passage:
At dinner in their Mumbai flat, Nazia announced, "I think homework should be banned till Class 8."
Her older sister Ganga snorted. "Says the girl who does hers at midnight. Brilliant logic."
Nazia felt the heat rise in her face. She wanted to snap back something about Ganga's marks. Instead she put her spoon down.
"Okay, my claim is: younger kids get more from play and sleep than from worksheets. Our school counsellor said Class 5 kids are coming in tired. And my cousin's school in Pune has no homework till Class 6, and their results are fine."
Ganga raised an eyebrow. "But some kids need practice at home, or they fall behind."
"That's a fair point," Nazia said. "So maybe short practice, not hours."
Their father looked impressed. Ganga shrugged. "Fine. That's actually a decent argument."
Nazia grinned into her dal.

qa.q: Where is the cousin's school that has no homework till Class 6?
qa.a: The cousin's school is in Pune.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Ganga mocked her?
qa.a: Nazia felt embarrassed and angry, her face heating up, and was tempted to hit back about Ganga's marks.

qa.q: What made Nazia's argument work?
qa.a: She stated a clear claim, gave evidence from the counsellor and her cousin's school, and admitted Ganga's fair point instead of ridiculing her.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt when Nazia called her point fair?
qa.a: Ganga was probably caught off guard and softened, since being acknowledged made it easier to admit the argument was decent.

grounding: The dinner scene shows a teenager building an argument with claims and evidence, acknowledging a good point, and ridicule failing.

passage:
"Uniforms kill self-expression," Wasim said, slapping the desk. "Forty kids dressed like photocopies. That's not a school, that's a factory."
"Can I answer?" Avni asked.
"You'll say discipline. Everyone says discipline."
"I wasn't going to say discipline."
Mrs Kaur raised a finger. "Wasim, let her finish."
"Fine."
"At my old school there was no uniform," Avni said. "Kids got teased every day for wearing the same two shirts. A uniform hid who could afford what."
The class went quiet. Wasim opened his mouth to laugh, then didn't.
"Okay," he said. "That's a real point. I hadn't thought about money."
"So you agree?"
"No. But maybe the answer isn't no uniform. Maybe it's a simple uniform plus one free-dress day a week, with a rule against teasing."
"That's... actually not bad."
Mrs Kaur wrote both points on the board. "Now that is a debate."

qa.q: What did Avni say happened at her old school?
qa.a: Kids got teased every day for wearing the same two shirts.

qa.q: What might Wasim have felt when he opened his mouth to laugh and didn't?
qa.a: Wasim probably felt caught off guard and a little humbled, since the point about money was new to him; he may also have felt some respect for an argument he hadn't expected.

qa.q: What went wrong at the start, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Wasim tried to win by slapping the desk and predicting Avni's answer; listening, admitting 'That's a real point' and adapting the idea turned it into a real debate.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when Wasim said 'Everyone says discipline'?
qa.a: Avni likely felt talked over and brushed off, which is why she had to ask to answer and then correct him.

grounding: It shows a teenager defending a view with claims, slipping into volume and ridicule, then acknowledging a good point and refining the argument.
